title: Twice a year at Amritsar
hook: the misls met as the Sarbat Khalsa at Vaisakhi and Diwali to decide together before the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Phulkian states, named for Phul: Patiala, Nabha and Jind, south of the river, sometimes counted with the misls and sometimes not. Your line was apart, yet related. Who did you reach out to? Today, the days when everyone came together. Day nine hundred.

Who decides, when nobody is king? The misl chiefs argued over villages and grazing and who owed whom. Some of them had fought each other. No ruler stood over them to settle it, and each answered to his own riders. Yet at Vaisakhi in spring and Diwali in autumn, Sikh histories say, they came to Amritsar, sat down together, and put the Guru Granth Sahib in front of them. Today: twice a year at Amritsar.
screen: `NOBODY IS KING.` → `RIVALS, EACH WITH HIS OWN RIDERS.` → `ONE PLACE, TWICE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: The gathering had a name: the Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat means all, the whole. So it was the whole Khalsa, not one chief's council, not a king's court. That's the first thing to notice. In principle, every band had a place in it. The second thing is where they sat. Tradition says the assembly met before the Guru Granth Sahib, near the Akal Takht. The scripture was not a decoration on the wall. It was the presence they were deciding in front of. And that changed the tone of the room. A chief who might shout in his own camp had to speak, here, as one Sikh among others before the Guru. The third thing is what came out of it. A decision reached this way was called a gurmata. Sikhs describe it as a resolution of the Guru, made by the gathered Khalsa in the Guru's presence. Once it was agreed, the bands were bound by it together. Sikh histories say this is how the misls chose shared leaders, planned joint campaigns, and set their quarrels aside, at least for a season. And notice the season. Vaisakhi and Diwali were already festival days, days for coming to Amritsar anyway. The meeting rode on the back of the celebration. People came to bathe in the pool and to see the Harmandir, and while they were there, they decided things. Faith first, then business, and the business done in faith's presence. A people with no single ruler found a way to have a single voice, twice a year. Decide before the Guru.
screen: `SARBAT KHALSA: THE WHOLE KHALSA.` · `SEATED BEFORE THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.` · `THE GURMATA BINDS EVERY BAND.` · `ON THE FESTIVAL DAYS.` · then, large: `DECIDE BEFORE THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a decision you share with someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one choice that isn't yours alone: something with a partner, a family, a team, a roommate. Notice how you usually make it. Do you decide and announce? Wait for someone else? Now picture sitting down with them in a quiet room, nobody shouting, with something larger than both of you present. What would you say differently? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
gurmata, a resolution agreed by the whole Khalsa before the Guru Granth Sahib, at the gatherings held twice a year at Amritsar, at Vaisakhi and Diwali, as the Sarbat Khalsa. Today's word.
Your line: decide before the guru. Today, make one shared decision slowly, sitting down, with everyone it touches given a turn to speak. Day nine hundred.

howItsDone: Sikhs still speak of the Sarbat Khalsa and the gurmata, and Sikh congregations take decisions before the Guru Granth Sahib, often ending with Ardas.

notes: Meeting 'near the Akal Takht' stated as tradition; confirm.
'Sarbat means all, the whole': a plain translation, kept because it carries the lesson; confirm.
'Sikh histories say this is how the misls chose shared leaders, planned joint campaigns, and set their quarrels aside': confirm the scope.
howItsDone mentions modern congregational decision-making before the Guru Granth Sahib; confirm.
Editor: rewrote the hook, which repeated day 887's image of riders converging on Amritsar from every direction; it now opens on the question of who decides when nobody is king.
Audit: cut the unsourced 'no band was too small to come and none too big to skip it' for 'in principle, every band had a place in it'.
